newsitem.title: USA: Lawyers jockey as tobacco trial gets underway.
newsitem.headline: Lawyers jockey as tobacco trial gets underway.

text.p: Six years after it was filed, a landmark secondhand smoke case went to trial Monday morning, with jury selection beginning and tobacco industry attorneys asking the judge to bar attorneys for both sides from talking to reporters.

"We ask that the court issue a gag order directing counsel on both sides not to speak to the press until the trial is over," David Hardy, attorney for Philip Morris Cos Inc and Loews Corp's Lorillard Inc, asked Dade County Circuit Judge Robert Kaye before the first group of 50 potential jurors entered the courtroom.
Kaye did not immediately rule on the request.

The case, known as Broin vs. Philip Morris et al, was filed on behalf of some 60,000 flight attendants, themselves non-smokers, who claim they contracted a variety of maladies, including lung cancer, from breathing cigarette smoke on U.S.-based passenger jets.

Potential jurors were given a questionnaire two weeks ago. Attorneys for both sides had reviewed their responses in recent days and met before the trial started, just after 1000 EDT/1400 GMT, to discuss which candidates should be summarily dismissed.
But none had been dismissed as the two sides argued over the order in which potential panelists should be questioned.

Tobacco industry attorneys said Susan Rosenblatt and some of the flight attendant plaintiffs had appeared on a morning television show, despite Kaye's order that attorneys be cautious in their comments to the media. Stanley Rosenblatt, co-counsel for the plaintiffs and Susan Rosenblatt's husband, responded that the comments by Mrs. Rosenblatt had been taped.
"I have given no interviews, live interviews, since the weekend or today," he said.

Rosenblatt also said that while the lead tobacco attorneys have not spoken to the press, industry officials have given statements. Dan Donahue, a senior vice president at R.J. Reynolds Tobacco, a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp, spoke at least twice to reporters in the courthouse media room on Monday.

Lead plaintiff Norma Broin attended the trial on Monday and said she was taking a vacation from her work as a flight attendant for AMR Corp's American Airlines to attend the trial. She said she was "ecstatic" that the trial was beginning.
Patty Young, another plaintiff who was a leader in the effort to ban cigarette smoking on most U.S. aircraft flights, also attended Monday.

"I'm overwhelmed with happiness that something's finally happening here," she said, expressing anger at the tobacco industry. "It makes me sick having to sit here with those tobacco people," she said, pointing toward the tobacco industry attorneys at the defense table and filling rows several rows along the left side of the courtroom.
